description: We are BurnBase, a team participating in the Bucharest Local Event for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our goal is to build a clean, practical POC application that harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS satellite hot spot data to track and visualize thermal anomalies and wildfires more accurately.
summary:
We built BurnBase to solve a clear gap in wildfire response and insurance risk. Right now, satellites like NASA FIRMS detect heat pixels several times a day, but a raw thermal dot on a map does not tell emergency teams which specific houses are in danger or give insurers a fast, verifiable financial risk number.

BurnBase puts everything into one live browser tool. It groups NASA FIRMS (VIIRS and MODIS) and EONET fire detections into verified clusters, pulls live wind and humidity data, and calculates where the fire is likely to spread over the next 6, 12, and 24 hours.
We then intersect those spread cones with real OpenStreetMap and Microsoft building footprints and roads. Civil defense teams get a 1.5 km roof-level view with NASA GIBS SWIR imagery and draft evacuation alerts, while insurers get an instant replacement-cost breakdown they can download and audit.
details:
What It Does and How It Works

BurnBase connects raw orbital wildfire detections to street-level emergency triage and auditable insurance exposure in a single browser tool. Right now, satellites detect heat pixels multiple times a day, but a thermal dot on a map does not tell emergency teams which specific houses are in danger or give insurers a fast, verifiable financial risk number.

BurnBase chains the entire workflow into four steps:

1. Multi-Sensor Verification: The app pulls near-real-time thermal detections from NASA FIRMS (VIIRS NOAA-20, VIIRS NOAA-21, and MODIS) alongside open wildfire events from NASA EONET v3. Instead of treating every isolated pixel as a major fire, it clusters detections across space and time, promoting only verified clusters with at least four detections, multi-pass or multi-satellite confirmation, and medium or higher confidence.

2. Live Weather and Spread Cones: For each verified cluster, BurnBase fetches live 10 m wind speed, direction, gusts, and relative humidity through a secure serverless proxy (Meteomatics with an automatic Open-Meteo fallback). It combines Fire Radiative Power, wind load, gusts, and fuel dryness into a 0 to 100 Hazard Score and projects directional 1-hour, 3-hour, and 6-hour spread cones using Turf.js geodesic math.

3. Parametric Insurance and Auditable Exposure: BurnBase intersects active fire footprints and wind cones with real OpenStreetMap and Microsoft Building Footprints plus major road networks. Under the Insurance tab, underwriters see exposed building area in square meters broken down by occupancy type (residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural) and clipped road length in kilometers, multiplied by transparent replacement-cost rates. Users can export a downloadable exposure report with the exact rates and data sources stated, building the objective hazard baseline needed for parametric triggers and rapid claims triage.

4. Civil Protection and 1.5 km Micro Inspector: Emergency managers see threatened assets grouped by arrival horizon (inside the fire, within 1 hour, 3 hours, or 6 hours) along with a structured DRAFT alert payload flagged for local authority verification. Opening Fire Impact launches a 1.5 km by 1.5 km Micro Inspector at roof-level zoom, overlaying NASA GIBS SWIR false-color layers and 24-hour thermal detections onto Esri World Imagery and flagging real structures within 250 m as Critical and within 1 km as Warning.

Benefits and Intended Impact

For insurers, MGAs, and reinsurers, BurnBase replaces slow black-box catastrophe delays with a fast, reproducible exposure figure tied directly to public satellite telemetry and real building polygons. For civil defense teams and municipalities, it cuts the time between a satellite pass and knowing which specific homes and evacuation routes lie downwind.

Tools, Languages, and Data Sources Used

We built BurnBase as a client-side web application using React 19, Vite, MapLibre GL JS for WebGL rendering, and Turf.js for geodesic hulls, buffers, and spatial intersections, backed by a lightweight serverless weather proxy (Vercel and Cloudflare Worker compatible) with no database required. Earth observation and geospatial layers come from NASA FIRMS, NASA EONET v3, NASA GIBS WMTS, Esri World Imagery, OpenStreetMap Overpass, Microsoft Building Footprints, Meteomatics, and Open-Meteo.

Creativity and Engineering Decisions

To keep a global geospatial console fast without a heavy backend, we implemented parallel multi-mirror Overpass queries with a two-minute circuit breaker, sequential NASA GIBS SWIR probing, and bounded spatial caches. Most importantly, we enforced strict data honesty: zero synthetic buildings are ever fabricated when rural map coverage is missing, demo archive playback is clearly labeled SIMULATION, and API credentials stay isolated on the server proxy.
dataRefs: NASA FIRMS (VIIRS NOAA-20/21 & MODIS Near-Real-Time Thermal Detections)
NASA EONET v3 (Earth Observatory Natural Event Tracker - Wildfires API)
NASA GIBS (Global Imagery Browse Services - VIIRS M11-I2-I1 & MODIS Terra 721 SWIR WMTS)
projectRefs: OpenStreetMap & Overpass API (Building Footprints, Critical Facilities & Road Networks)
Microsoft Building Footprints (Esri ArcGIS MSBFP2 Feature Service)
Esri World Imagery & Reference Labels (High-Resolution Satellite Basemap)
Meteomatics Weather API (10m Wind, Gusts, Temperature & Humidity)
Open-Meteo Weather Forecast API (Wind & Humidity Telemetry)
BigDataCloud Reverse Geocoding API (Incident Place Naming)
MapLibre GL JS (WebGL Geospatial Rendering Engine)
React, Vite & Lucide Icons (Open-Source Frontend Framework & Icons)
